analysis.one_liner: Limits corporate bankruptcies from cutting worker and retiree benefits and blocks executive bonuses.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it died without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten bankruptcy rules so that when a company goes broke, it can cut employee and retiree benefits only by the minimum needed to stay alive — and its executives' pay and health benefits would have to be cut by the same share. It would have paid retirees whose health coverage is cut two years of insurance premiums in cash, raised the amount of owed wages that get first-in-line priority from $10,000 to $25,000, banned bonus payments to company insiders during bankruptcy, and required bankruptcy cases to be filed where most workers and operations are located, rather than wherever the company chooses.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees and retirees of companies that file for bankruptcy. Their health benefits could only be cut to the minimum needed to keep the company alive, retirees whose coverage is cut would get two years of premiums for continuation coverage or an Affordable Care Act exchange plan, owed wages and benefits would carry higher priority (up to $25,000 and a full year of wages instead of $10,000 and 180 days), and retiree health benefits promised under collective bargaining would be presumed vested and untouchable unless the employer can prove workers were clearly told otherwise.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and retirees of bankrupt companies

how_it_helps.text: A company could reject a union contract or cut retiree health benefits only with the minimum modifications necessary to prevent liquidation, proven by clear and convincing evidence, and executives' benefits would have to be cut by at least the same percentage as employees'.

Retirees whose benefits are cut in bankruptcy would receive cash equal to two years of premiums for continuation coverage or a comparable plan on an Affordable Care Act exchange, with courts able to require more where fair.
The priority claim ceiling for unpaid wages and benefits would rise from $10,000 over 180 days to $25,000 over one year, and bonus payments to company insiders would be prohibited during bankruptcy.

Bankruptcy cases would have to be filed in the district where the largest share of employees, retirees, assets, and operations were located in the prior year, and a Comptroller General report would document how corporations use spin-offs, mergers, and bankruptcies to avoid paying promised benefits.

Retiree health benefits would be presumed fully vested and unmodifiable once an employee retires or completes 20 years of service, unless the employer shows by clear and convincing evidence the worker was told the benefits could be cut.

analysis.who_pays: Companies in financial distress and their executives. Reorganizing companies would face a higher bar for cutting labor costs, would have to keep paying required pension contributions during bankruptcy, could not pay insider bonuses, and could be forced to claw back compensation paid to insiders in the year before filing. Creditors and lenders in distressed-company cases would recover less as workers and retirees move up the repayment line.

drawbacks.text: Raising the bar for rejecting union contracts and mandating continued pension contributions could make reorganization more expensive or unworkable for some failing companies, pushing them into outright liquidation in which every employee loses their job.

Presuming retiree health benefits are vested for life after 20 years of service, with a clear-and-convincing standard to overcome it, would create large potential liabilities and litigation for employers and could discourage companies from offering retiree health coverage in the first place.

Requiring all insiders' benefits to be cut alongside employees' and banning all bonus payments removes flexibility that bankruptcy judges and companies sometimes use to retain key managers needed to run a reorganizing business.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections for workers and retirees are real and targeted at a specific, well-documented problem: companies using bankruptcy to shed promised benefits while executives keep their pay. The costs fall on distressed companies and their creditors, which is the point of the bill, but the strongest objection — that making reorganization more expensive could push marginal firms into liquidation, costing jobs — is a genuine tradeoff, and the lifetime-vesting presumption for retiree health benefits is written broadly enough that it could have generated expensive disputes well beyond the bankruptcy context.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate and sent to the Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator John Rockefeller introduced the bill on June 3, 2014, joined by Senator Elizabeth Warren.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever took place, and the bill expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that use bankruptcy to cut union contracts and retiree health benefits keep the existing rules, including the freedom to file in business-friendly courts and to pay insider bonuses during reorganization.

for.name: Sen. John D. Rockefeller IV
for.role: U.S. Senator from West Virginia; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to limit benefit cuts and insider bonuses in corporate bankruptcies.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only cosponsor.

against.name: Patrick Leahy
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no partisan split was recorded; its two supporters were both Democrats and no Republican cosponsored it.

industries.note: The bill would have raised the cost of shedding union contracts, retiree health benefits, and pension obligations in bankruptcy, banned insider bonuses, and clawed back recent insider compensation. Executives' interest in keeping pay and flexibility to cut worker benefits runs directly against employees and retirees.

Debtors sponsoring pension plans would have had to keep making required contributions after filing, with statutory liens for missed payments protected from avoidance. Responsible employers that never enter bankruptcy would see no change.

industries.industry: ERISA group health plan sponsors and administrators
industries.note: New summary-plan-description disclosures about whether benefits can be modified or terminated, plus the vested-benefits presumption, would add compliance and litigation exposure for plan sponsors.
